name: Green Apple
lede: Green Apple is a bright, highly saturated yellow-green named for the fruit's skin rather than its flesh, recorded by the 2010 xkcd color-name survey.

sections.title: The fruit's skin, not its flesh
sections.body:
Our library files Green Apple as a nature name, one of the plant and food words the 2010 xkcd color survey collected when it asked online visitors to type a name for colors shown on screen [1]. The name points to the skin of a tart green apple, such as a Granny Smith, rather than the paler, yellower flesh underneath [1].

The nearest named look-alikes on file are [[vibrant-green|Vibrant Green]], a touch more vivid, and [[apple|Fresh Green]], a shade duller [2]. [[apple-green|Apple Green]] is a separate, older entry and itself a duller, slightly different green, and [[kiwi|Kiwi Green]] is duller and lighter still [2]. In printed English the two-word phrase "green apple" was already common by 1800, for the fruit rather than the color, and the color sense only became common online after the 2010 survey [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,781-painting archive carries a color close enough to this one over enough of its canvas to count, as photographed [3]. That is expected: Green Apple is more saturated than most pigments artists before the twentieth century had access to, and our collection leans older and European [3].

questions.q: Green Apple is named for which part of the fruit?
True or false: Green Apple and Apple Green are the same name for the same shade.

openers: Green Apple is more saturated than almost any pigment available before the twentieth century, which is why old paintings never carry it.
